extracted.intended_audience: editorial/political cartoonists, newspaper editors, journalism students, and educators evaluating cartoon newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for determining whether an editorial/political cartoon is publishable, effective, and newsworthy for newspapers and other news outlets. Covers subject selection, formal qualities (clarity, symbolism, caricature), factual and ethical standards, timeliness, and award-quality attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of political/editorial cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: A political cartoon is a drawing made for editorial commentary on politics, politicians, and current events. Includes caricature, expresses opinion, requires audience knowledge of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets scope: work should be an explicitly opinionated visual commentary aimed at current political subjects; assumes audience familiarity with the subject and often uses caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Subjects that get cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: Major news event of the day/week; political controversy; government scandal; policy debate topic; election cycle moments; international crisis; social movement moment; cultural figure in news; anniversary of important event; local political news (in local press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons should tie to subjects that are timely and of public interest; local presses may prioritise local political news. Use these subject-types to judge whether an idea merits a cartoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject clearly identified; visual references readable; audience can decode without explanation; caption (if any) clarifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cartoon must be immediately legible to its intended audience — avoid cryptic imagery. Visual elements should communicate the subject and message without requiring outside explanation; captions can be used to clarify but should not be crutches for an unclear visual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive Argument
rubrics_metrics.description: "More than a slogan" — invites consideration of argument; visual + written features make case; reasons to support view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A publishable cartoon should do more than state an opinion; it should present an argument or viewpoint that prompts thought. Combine visual metaphor and any text to give reasons or an angle rather than only a snappy one-liner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoonist may exaggerate but may NOT alter facts; quotes accurately attributed; people depicted as recognizable selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire permits exaggeration of traits, but not fabrication of factual claims. Ensure depicted facts (dates, attributions, basic events) are accurate to avoid libel/misleading the audience; recognizable depiction supports identification but shouldn't falsify reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Single item / issue; clearly identified; simplification (but not distortion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cartoons concentrate on one clear target or issue to avoid muddled messaging. Simplify complex matters to make a point, but do not distort central facts or misrepresent the subject to the point of inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective visual symbols; universally understood (within target audience); original or apt cliche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbols that will be understood by the audience and that strengthen the argument; either offer fresh symbolic choices or use familiar symbols in an apt way. Avoid obscure or culturally-specific symbols that the target readership won't decode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizable subject; exaggerates real features; avoids racist / cruel depiction (modern standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration should aid identification and commentary but must not cross into demeaning, racist, or gratuitously cruel portrayals. Maintain dignity when possible and be sensitive to modern standards around race, ethnicity, gender and other protected characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tied to current event; time-sensitive humor; shelf-life matched to event significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons should connect clearly to current news or anniversaries so their humor and comment are relevant; consider how long the joke will remain meaningful and whether the event's significance justifies shorter or longer shelf-life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid stereotypes (race, ethnicity, religion, gender); distinguish satire from libel; comment on actions, not appearance unfairly; punch up, not down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical evaluation includes avoiding harmful stereotypes and ensuring critique targets actions/power rather than marginalized identities. Verify that satirical claims cannot be reasonably read as factual falsehoods that could be libelous. Prefer targets with power ('punch up') rather than vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit newsworthiness criteria for cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: News event timeliness; symbolic capacity of subject; visual potential (iconic face/situation); public knowledge of event; argumentative angle available; humor / satire opportunity; restraint from cruelty; brevity of message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These implicit factors help editors judge whether an idea will work as a cartoon: it should lend itself to clear visual treatment, be within the public's awareness, offer a discernible angle or punchline, and allow concise expression without cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulitzer (Illustrated Reporting and Commentary) editorial cartooning criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong drawing skill; pictorial effect; editorial effectiveness; originality; public service value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award-level cartoons are expected to combine high technical drawing ability and strong visual impact with clear editorial force, originality of approach, and contribution to public understanding or discourse.
